NEW YORK, May 15 (P.-A.)

Federal judge has ruled that the United States Communist Party and its Daily Worker can't escape paying taxes on the ground that the payment would put them out of business,

"No entity has a right to restrain the collection of taxes on the mere ground that continuance of such entity is threatened," Judge Richard H. Levet declared yesterday.

The ruling cleared the way for the Internal Revenue Service to collect tax assessments from the party and its newspaper.

Judge Levet denied motions by counsel for the party and newspaper for an order to restrain Ronald C. Moysey, district revenue director for Lower Manhattan, from collecting further money to satisfy the tax judgments.

Subject to Laws

The judge said:

"There is no inherent right in any organization to avoid payment of taxes solely by reason of the fact that it may be engaged in publicity efforts which will perforce cease if it neglects or refuses to pay its taxes.

"A newspaper is subject to the same general laws of the United States as is any other industry conducted for profit. The fact that the Daily Worker may be forced to discontinue publication is hardship which is no reason for this court's equitable intervention."

The judge said he found no violation of due process or invasion of the freedom of the press in the tax case.

The Communist Party, contending that other political organizations are not taxed, charged it was being denied "equal protection under the law."

Contention Is Denied

To this contention the judge answered:

"No facts are shown in any of the legal papers submitted here that other political parties have a like organization, like financial record and like sources of income."

The Treasury Department last March assessed the Communist Party $386,265 and the Daily Worker $46,047 in back taxes.

Judge Levet ruled that his court had no power to review the assessments.

After the Communist Party and the Daily Worker are officially notified of Judge Levet's ruling, they will have 80 days to petition the United States Tax Court for a review.

Brief seizures of party and Daily Worker properties followed the levying of the assessments. Publication of the Daily Worker was not interrupted.

An urgent request that construction time on a second airport at Burke, Va., be cut to two years will be contained in a recommendation to the Senate Commerce Committee, it was learned today.

Most estimates on the proposed Burke airport have set five years as the time necessary to bring it to full completion. Planes could be operating in three, however, but all installations would not be included.

Senator Monroney, Democrat of Oklahoma, chairman of the aviation subcommittee, said yesterday the report recommending the Burke location is being prepared for the full committee.

Would Ask Funds at Once
Commerce Undersecretary Rothschild yesterday reiterated his department's willingness to ask immediately for go-ahead funds when the final decision on the airport location is made. He first presented the Commerce idea during testimony before the subcommittee last Monday.

Joint use of Andrews was the Commerce Department's first choice in a report submitted to Congress January 3. The Air Force strongly opposes the proposal, saying the full facilities of the big air base are needed in the air defenses of Washington.

Senator Monroney has consistently opposed—even ridiculed—the Commerce proposal listing Andrews as the number one site. He has used it as ammunition in his campaign to divorce the Civil Aeronautics Administration from Commerce and establish it as an independent agency. It also has been brought into the Senator's inquiry over the firing of former CAA Administrator Frederick B. Lee, who resigned in December.

The subcommittee reports recommendation for a "crash program" to complete the Burke airport in two years would involve double stage construction, with several contracting firms operating simultaneously, Senator Monroney said.

Fight Is Certain
How much of a fight will develop in Congress over the Burke recommendation is problematical but one thing is certain—there's going to be one.

The Maryland congressional delegation has constantly opposed Burke—or any other place—in favor of Baltimore's Friendship International. But even Commerce rejected the Friendship suggestion.

Undersecretary Rothschild said in his Monday testimony that $3.5 million will be needed immediately to start the Burke construction, most of it for additional engineering.

The Government already has spent close to a million for property acquisition at Burke, but Congress all but junked the project by cutting off additional money.

There is strong opposition at the resident level in Fairfax County against Burke, but it is running into powerful competition from the Committee for Burke Airport. The committee has the backing of scores of business and civic organizations, including Chambers of Commerce and real estate organizations.

Industrial Growth Cited
The committee's officials refute arguments of Burke opponents that the project would be detrimental to the whole of Fairfax County by citing industrial growth which has surrounded other new airports in the Nation.

Representative Broyhill, Republican of Virginia, whose district includes Fairfax, has opposed the Burke location, contending that the disadvantages would outweigh the economic advantages cited by proponents.

dent Truman have been tell
ing the American farmers they
are in a bad way and they had
better vote against Eisenhower
and the Republicans. So far,
there has been no evidence
that Adlai Stevenson, Estes Ke-

set the prairies afire.


Republican leaders, however,
are well aware that in 1952,
when the election seemed in
the bag for their presidential
candidate, Thomas E. Dewey,
it was the Midwest farmers
and those in California and
home of the other far Western
States who really threw the
election to the then President
Truman. They are not taking

President Eisenhower himself
is going out to Iowa, heart of
the Corn Belt, for the national
blowing contest September 8, and a few days later will
deliver a first major campaign
address on the problems of the
farmers and what he is doing
about them.


Not only could the fate of
the Republican national ticket
be determined by the farm
vote, but also that vote could
decide the political complexion
of the new Congress which is
to be elected. Thirteen Re-
publican Senators are up for
reelection in States where the
farm vote plays a most im-
portant part, a half dozen of
them in the great prairie States
of the Midwest. The Republi-
cans, too, have a large num-
ber of House members to elect
and re-elect in the farm States,
if they are to have a chance of
controlling Congress.


What Recent Poll Shows


A recently published poll in
Wallace's Farmer and Home-
stead—widely read farm pub-
lication in Iowa—indicates
that many farmers have not
made up their minds—or had
not, just before the national
conventions—how they will
vote. It also indicated that too
many of the farmers might not
be enough interested to go to
the polls and vote November
6. It is this seeming indiffer-

Democrats have insisted for
long time the farmers, because
of low prices, were ready to
leap on their band wagon. In

farm vote to pull the Steven-
